name: slider
title: Slider
description: A value chosen by dragging a handle along a rail. The sheet has no slider in it, so this is an invention — and it is the progress bar's drawing made interactive: the same 4px rail, the same accent fill, the same progress.ts. A slider is a bar with a handle on it, and two drawings of one idea is the drift that file exists to prevent.

files.content:
/**
 * The field anatomy, shared by every control that wears it — `TextField`,
 * `SearchField`, and the textarea, select, checkbox and radio still to come.
 *
 * The styling lives here, and so does the one piece of field *state* React Aria
 * leaves to us: the validation context `Slider` — the one field it does not treat
 * as a field — publishes for its own `Error` slot. See
 * `FieldValidationContext` at the bottom of this file.
 *
 * Each component defines its own slot components, thin as they are, so that its
 * docs and manifest describe its own API rather than pointing at another
 * component's.
 */
import { createContext } from 'react'

/**
 * The three control sizes. `size` is set once on the field and travels as two
 * custom properties rather than through React context: the control, and any
 * affix inside it, are ordinary descendants of the field, so inheritance already
 * does the work. It also means a one-off override is just a utility on the
 * element rather than a new prop.
 */
export type FieldSize = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'

export const FIELD_SIZES: Record<FieldSize, string> = {
  sm: '[--field-control-h:2.25rem] [--field-control-text:0.8125rem]', // 36px / 13px
  md: '[--field-control-h:2.75rem] [--field-control-text:0.875rem]', // 44px / 14px
  lg: '[--field-control-h:3.25rem] [--field-control-text:0.9375rem]', // 52px / 15px
}

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-field`: legend, control, then the hint that explains it.
 *
 * The `font-size` here is what the control and any affix inherit. It sits on the
 * field rather than on the input so it still reaches an affix, which is the
 * input's sibling — a `cap`-sized icon would otherwise match the page's font
 * instead of the field's.
 *
 * The two border properties are published here for the same reason `Checkbox`
 * publishes its own: read-only lives on the field root, while the border it changes
 * is on the input, and a group variant cannot win that cascade — see the note on
 * `INPUT`. Declaring them here means the input only reads them, and the ordinary
 * cascade decides, because `[data-readonly]` plainly outranks the bare declaration.
 */
export const FIELD = [
  'group flex flex-col gap-2 [font-size:var(--field-control-text)]',
  '[--field-border:var(--color-input)]',
  '[--field-hover:var(--color-border)]',
  // Read-only is not disabled: the value is the whole point of the field, so it
  // keeps full-strength text. Only the affordances go — a quieter hairline, and no
  // brightening on hover — because there is nothing here to invite a click on.
  'data-[readonly]:[--field-border:var(--color-border-soft)]',
  'data-[readonly]:[--field-hover:var(--color-border-soft)]',
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-affix` wrapper. `Group` exists for one case: an affix is
 * positioned against the control, but the field also holds the legend and the
 * hint, so an affix anchored to the field would centre on all three.
 * Wrapping the control gives the affix the right box — and it stays opt-in, so a
 * plain field has no extra element at all.
 *
 * The two `:has()` rules are here for the same reason: the room an affix needs is
 * padding on the input, and the group is what can see both of them. The input
 * itself never has to know it has neighbours.
 */
export const GROUP = [
  'relative flex w-full',
  'has-[[data-slot=icon-start]]:[&>[data-slot=input]]:ps-10.5', // 42px, per the sheet's search field
  'has-[[data-slot=icon-end]]:[&>[data-slot=input]]:pe-14', // 56px, per the sheet's trailing unit
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`: 12px, uppercase, letterspaced, white 70%.
 *
 * The required marker is drawn from the field's own `data-required`, so the label
 * never has to be told and the asterisk cannot drift out of sync with
 * `isRequired`. The input already carries the native `required`, so this is the
 * visual half of the same fact.
 */
export const LABEL = [
  'text-[12px] uppercase tracking-[0.04em] text-muted-foreground',
  "group-data-[required]:after:ms-1 group-data-[required]:after:text-destructive group-data-[required]:after:content-['*']",
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-input`.
 *
 * The resting hairline is what identifies the control. The sheet gives
 * `.ds-input` a transparent border and leaves the panel-2 fill to do the job, but
 * that fill is 1.23:1 on the dark page and 1.17:1 on the light one, so the field is
 * nearly invisible as a boundary in both. `--input` is the smallest
 * hairline that clears the 3:1 a control boundary needs on each.
 *
 * Hover has to *strengthen* it rather than replace it: the sheet's hover is white
 * at 25%, which is now weaker than the resting line and would erase it.
 *
 * `outline-none` on focus suppresses the *browser's* ring, which is what the
 * sheet's `.ds-input:focus { outline: none }` is really doing. Chrome gives a
 * focused text input its `:focus-visible` ring at `outline-style: auto` regardless
 * of React Aria's attribute, so leaving it alone means a blue UA ring on a teal
 * system. Focus is then the border alone — adding the shared 3px-offset ring here
 * would draw two parallel teal hairlines with a gap, which reads as a fault.
 * `Button` can carry that ring because the edge it repeats is a solid fill.
 */
export const INPUT = [
  // **The corner is a token now, and `rounded-md` is the control step of its scale.** Pulse's own
  // `--radius` is `0`, so the sheet's square field is unchanged here; a theme that sets a radius
  // moves every control in the library at once. See the radius note in `docs/theming.md`.
  'w-full font-mono rounded-md border border-(--field-border)',
  'h-(--field-control-h) px-3.5',
  'bg-muted text-foreground placeholder:text-foreground/35',
  'transition-[border-color,background-color] duration-(--duration-fast) ease-pulse',
  // Focus and invalid stay literal, so they outrank the published border and always
  // win — including on a read-only field, which is still focusable and still the
  // field the caret should be able to reach.
  'data-[hovered]:not-data-[focused]:border-(--field-hover)',
  'data-[focused]:outline-none data-[focused]:border-primary',
  'data-[invalid]:not-data-[focused]:border-destructive',
  // The browser already knows when someone has left a field invalid, so the state needs no
  // "touched" class and no blur listener — it only needed a rule. Same line in `TextArea`.
  'user-invalid:not-data-[focused]:border-destructive',
  'data-[disabled]:cursor-not-allowed data-[disabled]:opacity-40',
  // Read-only gets the cursor and nothing else that dims it. `opacity` here would
  // take the *value* down with it — at 40% the text measures 3.42:1, under the 4.5:1
  // body text needs, so the one thing the user came to read becomes the thing they
  // cannot.
  'group-data-[readonly]:cursor-not-allowed',
].join(' ')

/** The sheet's `.ds-hint`: 12px, tighter tracking, white 55%. */
export const HINT = 'text-[12px] tracking-[-0.5px] text-foreground/55'

/**
 * The sheet paints its error state yellow, because the original design had only
 * two accents and yellow was the nearest thing to a warning it owned. That does
 * not carry over here: `--warning` is this system's `secondary` button, so
 * errors would be the same colour as a secondary action. The error state uses
 * `--destructive`, the danger hue, and keeps the sheet's flex so an icon can be
 * dropped in front of the message.
 */
export const ERROR =
  'flex items-center gap-1.5 text-[12px] tracking-[-0.5px] text-destructive'

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-affix__unit` and `.ds-affix__icon`: pinned to the control's
 * box, vertically centred, and never a click target — the affix is decoration, and
 * a pointer-events-owning overlay would swallow clicks meant for the field. Sized
 * in `cap` like `Button.Icon`, so one icon works at every field `size`.
 */
export const ICON = [
  'absolute inset-y-0 z-10 grid place-items-center pointer-events-none',
  'text-foreground/70',
  '[&>svg]:block [&>svg]:h-[1.5cap] [&>svg]:w-auto [&>svg]:shrink-0',
].join(' ')

/** The sheet insets both affixes 14px from their edge. */
export const ICON_POSITIONS = {
  start: 'start-3.5',
  end: 'end-3.5',
} as const

export type IconPosition = keyof typeof ICON_POSITIONS

/**
 * The invalid state of a control React Aria does not treat as a field, published by that control
 * itself.
 *
 * **Every other field here reads its invalid state from React Aria.** `TextField`, `Select`,
 * `Switch` and the rest are handed `isInvalid`, and React Aria publishes the
 * `FieldErrorContext` their `Error` slot renders from. `Slider` is left out of that anatomy:
 * `useSlider` takes no `isInvalid` at all, and a slider *thumb*'s is deprecated with no
 * replacement — which is why this component's docs never showed a `FieldError`. (`TokenField` is
 * left out for the same reason and stays out: its message can be neither rendered nor reached. See
 * docs/components/tokenfield.md.)
 *
 * So `Slider` publishes the context itself, from an `isInvalid` prop the caller owns. That is
 * exactly what an integration binding a slider to a form has: a value it validated and a failure it
 * has to report. What it is *not* is React Aria's form validation — the `validationErrors` a
 * `Form` carries are keyed by field name and read by React Aria's own fields, and a slider never
 * sees them.
 *
 * **`errorId` is minted by the control, not by the slot**, because the message and the element it
 * describes are two different slots and only the control can own the name they share.
 */
export const FieldValidationContext = createContext<FieldValidation | null>(
  null,
)

export interface FieldValidation {
  /** Whether the control's value is invalid. */
  isInvalid: boolean
  /** The id the control's error message wears, so the control is described by the message. */
  errorId: string
}

/**
 * The `ValidityState` of a field nothing is wrong with — React Aria's own shape for "there is no
 * native input to ask", which is the situation for a slider.
 *
 * It is never read: `FieldError` looks only at `isInvalid` and `validationErrors`, and the
 * rest travels to a render-function child that never asks. It is here because React Aria types the
 * context as a `ValidationResult`, and a field that claims to be valid should carry a valid
 * object rather than a cast.
 */
export const VALID: ValidityState = {
  badInput: false,
  customError: false,
  patternMismatch: false,
  rangeOverflow: false,
  rangeUnderflow: false,
  stepMismatch: false,
  tooLong: false,
  tooShort: false,
  typeMismatch: false,
  valid: true,
  valueMissing: false,
}

/**
 * The sheet has no bar of any kind, so this is an invention — but a small one, and it borrows the
 * sheet's own language: square, hairline-thin, and its semantic colours rather than a new palette.
 *
 * Every constant here is shared by `ProgressBar` and `Meter`, the same split as `field.ts` between
 * `TextField`, `SearchArea` and `SearchField`. A progress bar and a meter are the same drawing of two
 * different facts, and the drawing is the thing that must not drift.
 */

/** The column: a header line, then the rail. */
export const PROGRESS = 'flex flex-col gap-2'

/** Label on the left, reading on the right — the sheet's own arrangement in a table row. */
export const HEADER = 'flex items-baseline justify-between gap-3'

/** The sheet's field legend, quieter than the value it names. */
export const LABEL =
  'text-[12px] uppercase tracking-[0.04em] text-foreground/55'

/** The reading, in the sheet's tabular figures so it does not jitter as it counts. */
export const VALUE = 'text-[12px] tabular-nums text-foreground/70'

/**
 * The empty part of a rail: a wash of the text colour rather than a panel, so it reads as the
 * unfinished part of the same thing. **Shared with `Slider`, which draws the same rail** — and it is
 * the wash that is shared, not the clip below it.
 */
export const TRACK_WASH = 'bg-foreground/12'

/**
 * The bar's rail. 4px, because a bar is a measurement and a 1px one is a hairline that happens to be
 * coloured — the reader cannot tell how full it is.
 *
 * The clip belongs to the **bar**, where the fill is the whole drawing. It is not part of what
 * a rail is: a slider's handle is 20px square on a 4px rail, and inheriting this clip painted it as a
 * 4px sliver. See `Slider`'s `RAIL` for the measurement.
 */
export const TRACK = 'relative h-1 w-full overflow-clip ' + TRACK_WASH

/**
 * The bar. Its width is a **value**, not a style — which is why it arrives as `--fill` and the
 * width stays a utility: `w-(--fill)` is in the class list like every other measurement here, and
 * the only thing written inline is the number React Aria computed.
 */
export const FILL = [
  'h-full w-(--fill)',
  'transition-[width] duration-(--duration-slow) ease-pulse',
].join(' ')

/**
 * What the bar is filled with. `accent` is a progress bar's — the thing being done wears the
 * system's one accent, as it does everywhere else. The other four are a meter's, and they are the
 * sheet's own semantic colours: a meter says how much, and how much is the only thing that decides
 * whether it is good news.
 */
export const TONE: Record<string, string> = {
  accent: 'bg-primary',
  success: 'bg-success',
  warning: 'bg-warning',
  danger: 'bg-destructive',
  neutral: 'bg-secondary',
}

/**
 * Indeterminate is not a value, so there is no width to draw. React Aria renders
 * `isIndeterminate` as the **absence** of `aria-valuenow`, and `percentage` arrives `undefined`
 * rather than `0` — which is the difference between "we do not know how far along this is" and "it
 * has not started". The bar fills the rail and pulses.
 *
 * A moving stripe would say it better, and it would need keyframes this system does not have. The
 * pulse is Tailwind's own, which means nothing new was invented to say "in progress".
 */
export const INDETERMINATE = 'motion-safe:animate-pulse'

docs:
A value chosen by dragging a handle along a rail. **The sheet has no slider in it**, so this is an
invention — and it is the progress bar's drawing made interactive: the same 4px rail, the same accent
fill, the same `progress.ts`. A slider _is_ a bar with a handle on it, and two drawings of one idea is
the drift that file exists to prevent.

```tsx
<Slider defaultValue={60}>
  <Slider.Header>
    <Slider.Label>Alert threshold</Slider.Label>
    <Slider.Value />
  </Slider.Header>
  <Slider.Track>
    <Slider.Fill />
    <Slider.Thumb />
  </Slider.Track>
</Slider>
```

| Slot            | React Aria     | Notes                                                            |
| --------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Slider`        | `Slider`       | The value. `size` is `sm \| md \| lg`, and `orientation`         |
| `Slider.Header` | —              | The label and the reading on one line                            |
| `Slider.Label`  | `Label`        | Names the rail — React Aria wires it, so there is no prop        |
| `Slider.Value`  | `SliderOutput` | An `<output>`, which is the element for a control's result       |
| `Slider.Track`  | `SliderTrack`  | The rail. One `Fill` and one or more `Thumb`s                    |
| `Slider.Fill`   | `SliderFill`   | The filled part — the run to the thumb, or between two           |
| `Slider.Thumb`  | `SliderThumb`  | A handle. `index` and `label` for a range                        |
| `Slider.Error`  | `FieldError`   | The message while `isInvalid` — React Aria supplies no such slot |

## The one field React Aria does not supply

`Slider` is not a field in React Aria. `useSlider` takes no `isInvalid` at all, a slider _thumb_'s is
`@deprecated` with no replacement, and the component's own docs never mention `FieldError` — so
there is no validation context for a slot to render from and no form message for it to show. Two things
follow, and both are this library's rather than React Aria's:

- **`isInvalid` is a prop of `Slider`.** It is what a form that has bound a slider to a value it
  validated has, and what React Aria cannot give it. `Slider` publishes the field contexts itself
  from that prop: the `FieldErrorContext` a `FieldError` renders from, and the
  `FieldValidationContext` in `field.ts` that carries the id the message and the thumb share.
- **The message is the caller's.** Every other `Error` slot in this library can be left empty and will
  show whatever React Aria's own validation produced; this one shows its children. There is no React
  Aria validation for a slider to surface, so that is the whole of what it can be given.

**The invalid state has to reach the input, not only the eye.** The grip turns `--destructive` — the
loudest mark on the rail — through a variable for the same reason `--slider-dim` is one: `data-invalid`
is on the root and the grip is a descendant. And the thumb hands `isInvalid` and the message's id to
React Aria's `SliderThumb`, whose range input is the element a screen reader reads the value from:
`aria-invalid="true"`, with `aria-describedby` pointing at the message. **`isInvalid` is deprecated
on a slider thumb with no replacement, and it is still the only thing that reaches that input.** The
grip is a picture; a message a screen reader cannot be pointed at is a message for sighted users only.
The assertion that keeps this honest reads the input's own attributes, not the painted grip.

### A range is the same component, twice

`Slider.Track` holds as many thumbs as you write, and React Aria keeps them from crossing.
**Each thumb's accessible name is its own label _plus_ the group's** — `"From Latency window"`, not
`"From"`. That is the right answer: a screen reader crossing a form hears which window _and_ which
end of it. A story therefore matches on a prefix rather than on a name invented to make it pass.

### `size` was accepted and ignored — twice

The same trap as the number field's steppers, one component later, and it survived two rounds because
the assertion only ever checked one end of it.

The first version set `h-1` outright, so `size` changed the legend's type and nothing else; `Sizes`
found three identical rails where it expected three. The rail was then wired to `--slider-rail` — and
the **handle** kept a fixed size, so three rails of three different thicknesses all carried an
identical grip, and `Sizes` still passed, because it was only looking at the rails.
`size-(--slider-thumb)` silently produced nothing; `h-(--slider-rail)` had worked the whole time.

The lesson is about the _test_ rather than the class: **check both ends of a two-ended decision.**
`Sizes` now asserts three distinct rail heights _and_ three distinct grip heights, and that every grip
is square. (It required the opposite for a while — "taller than it is wide" — which is the assertion the
section below is about.)

### Disabled dims through a variable, for the fourth time

`data-disabled` is on the slider **root** while the handle is a descendant, so a
`data-[disabled]:opacity-30` on the handle never matches and the handle stayed at full strength. The
root publishes `--slider-dim` and the handle reads it — the same shape as `Checkbox`'s indicator and
`Select`'s trigger. React Aria also renders an **inner wrapper** inside the thumb, so the input's
parent is not the styled element; `data-slot="thumb"` is the hook, as it is on the fill.

### The story that matters most measures the handle

`ThumbPosition` compares the handle's centre against the rail's width and expects a quarter. That is
the whole claim a slider makes, and the one a broken layout keeps while every behavioural assertion
still passes.

## The handle: square, full-strength, and the loudest mark on the rail

| size | rail | handle |
| ---- | ---- | ------ |
| `sm` | 3px  | 16px   |
| `md` | 4px  | 20px   |
| `lg` | 6px  | 24px   |

The sheet has no slider — this is one of the components invented here — so the handle's shape and colour
were choices, and it took three readings of the rendered control to get them right.

**Shape.** It began as a `bg-background` square **with a border**, which on the dark page was a black box showing
nothing but its own hairline. The verdict was that squareness was at fault, so it became a tall narrow bar —
7×18px at `md`, then 10×24px. The next reader said it still looked wrong, rightly: a bar a hairline wide and
several rails tall reads as a **cursor**, not as something a hand closes around. The border and the black fill
were the original problem; being square never was.

**What kept it a bar was an assertion.** `Sizes` required `height > width`, annotated "that proportion is what
makes it a grip" — so the wrong shape was not merely accepted, it was _enforced_, and no amount of looking at
the component would have found that.

**Colour, which was the actual complaint.** `bg-foreground/70` is 70% white: measurably lighter than the page, but
_duller than the teal fill it sits on_ — so on the filled half of the rail the handle receded while the fill
led, and it was hard to see. It is the thing you grab; it should be the loudest mark on the rail. It is now
`bg-foreground` at full strength, which reads against both the teal fill and the dark track with no border and no ring.
Sizes moved up one step at the same time.

**The state signals are scale, not colour.** With the handle already white at rest, hover and drag have nothing
left to brighten, so they grow. Dragging used to turn the handle **teal** — the exact colour of the fill
underneath it, invisible on the filled half. The same mistake as the resting colour, found in the same pass.

All three sizes carry the same rule, and `Sizes` checks that they are still three different sizes.

## The handle was painted as a sliver, and it hung above the rail

The grip the section above describes was not what the browser drew, and it took a 3× screenshot of the
rendered control to see it. Two separate faults, both from `Slider.Track` composing the progress bar's
recipe instead of its own:

1. **The rail clips.** `progress.ts` exports `TRACK` as clipping (`overflow-clip` now, `overflow-hidden`
   when this was found), which the bar can afford —
   its fill is the whole drawing. A slider's handle is a **20px square on a 4px rail**, so the clip painted
   it as a 4px white notch at the end of the fill. React Aria's own docs CSS for a slider track has no
   overflow rule at all. What the two rails share is the **wash**, not the clip; that is now its own
   export, `TRACK_WASH`.
2. **The handle had no cross-axis centre.** React Aria positions the thumb along the rail and centres it
   with `transform: translate(-50%, -50%)` — which assumes the box it translates already _starts_ at the
   rail's centre, and it does not, because `top` is `auto`. Measured, the grip sat **10px above** a 4px
   rail, hanging over the fill like a tab. React Aria's docs CSS carries the missing line: `top: 50%`
   when the rail lies down, `left: 50%` when it stands up. It is read off the **track**, because React Aria
   publishes `data-orientation` there and not on the thumb.

**Neither was visible to the suite, and the reason is the same for both.** Every assertion measured
`getBoundingClientRect`, which returns a layout box whether or not an ancestor clips it and whatever the
box's transform has done to it on screen: the handle measured 20×20 while painting four pixels tall. The
story now asserts the two mechanisms rather than the symptom — the track's computed `overflow` is
`visible`, the handle is taller than the rail, and its centre is within a pixel of the rail's in **both**
orientations. That is the difference between a component that works and one that only measures as if it
did.
